fields.meta_title: Free Anonymous Feedback Form Builder | Emergent
fields.meta_description: Build an anonymous feedback form that stores no names or emails. Emergent hides small-group results and delivers replies by case code.
fields.h1: Build an Anonymous Feedback Form That Stores No Names
fields.hero_description: Describe who gives feedback and who reads it. Emergent builds the anonymous feedback form, keeps identity out of the database and lets writers check for a reply with a private code.
fields.features_heading: What Keeps a Feedback Form Anonymous
fields.features_subheading: Most leaks come from what a form records quietly. These six choices decide what your database can say about who answered.
fields.feature_1:
No name or email field to fill in

Leave identity out of the form itself. Emergent builds it without a name or email field, and nobody signs in. The table behind it has no column where a name could ever be stored.
fields.feature_2:
IP addresses kept out of storage

Tell Emergent not to save IP addresses or device details with an answer. Each row holds the answer and the date it arrived, and nothing a log search could tie back to the writer.
fields.feature_3:
Replies through a private case code

Give every submission a random case code. The writer keeps it, managers reply against it, and the writer reads the reply later by entering the code. Nobody learns who asked.
fields.feature_4:
Results held below a group minimum

Set the fewest answers a report needs before anyone sees it, such as four. A smaller team stays hidden or rolls up into its department, and every filter in the results view obeys it.
fields.feature_5:
Comments checked for names first

Check each comment against your staff or resident list before readers see it. A comment that names someone waits for an editor to remove the name, and the rest go straight through.
fields.feature_6:
Code your security team can read

Export the full codebase to GitHub on paid plans. Your IT team can read exactly what the form stores before launch, and you can host it on your own servers if policy calls for that.

fields.usecase_heading: Where Feedback Arrives Without a Name
fields.tab_content_1:
Every reply goes to a code, not a name

Saltbrook Kitchen runs 3 restaurants and one suggestion form, opened from a QR code by each time clock. The form asks for no name or email and saves no IP address. Each submission gets a case code, such as PINE-4417. When the general manager replies, the cook who wrote in reads it by entering that code.
fields.tab_content_2:
No manager report with fewer than four answers

Tallgrass Analytics asks every team to rate its manager each spring and fall. A report stays hidden until at least 4 direct reports have answered, since one comment in a tiny sample is easy to pick out. Theo Lund's team of 5 has 3 answers, and his report is held. The other 8 managers already see theirs.
fields.tab_content_3:
When the form closes Friday, 31 of 42 have answered

Dr. Lena Ortiz asks her Statistics 210 class for anonymous feedback at midterm. The form records the date of each answer but not the time, which keeps a response from being matched to whoever left the lecture hall last. Results open once it closes. Lab length is the most common theme, raised in 14 comments.
fields.tab_content_4:
A neighbor's name in a comment holds it for review

Larkspur Commons, an HOA of 120 homes, gathers comments for a monthly board digest. The app checks each one against the resident directory first. A comment that names a neighbor waits for Rosa Kim, the community manager, to take the name out. This month 18 comments reached the board and 1 was held.

fields.howto_title: How to Create an Anonymous Feedback Form
fields.howto_description: Most of the work is deciding what the form must never keep. Settle that before you write a single question.
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Cut every field that points to a person
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Pick the smallest group you will report
fields.howto_step_1_des: Staff writing about a manager need more cover than customers rating a delivery. Write down who answers, who reads the results and what could happen to someone identified. That tells you how strict the form must be, and whether anonymous is the right choice at all.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Remove name and email first, then look at the quieter fields. Location and shift each look harmless, but on a team of six, the two together can single someone out. Keep only the fields the reader will act on, and cut the rest.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Choose a minimum number of answers below which results stay hidden, such as four. Teams under the minimum roll up into their department instead of showing alone. Agree on the number with whoever reads the reports, and write it down before launch.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Anonymous does not have to mean silent. Decide whether writers get a case code to check for a reply, whether answers go on a board everyone can read, or both. Write the first reply now, before any feedback arrives, and set who owns each topic.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Put the fields and storage rules into one prompt, along with the group minimum and the reply method. Emergent builds the form and its database table, plus a results view for whoever reads feedback. Change any rule later by asking for it in plain English.
fields.howto_step_6_title: 06 Route each topic to one owner
fields.howto_step_6_des: Connect Slack or email so new feedback reaches the person who answers it. Kitchen equipment goes to the general manager and course pacing to the teaching assistant. Each alert carries the comment and its topic, and nothing about who sent it.
fields.howto_step_7_title: 07 Test it the way a skeptic would
fields.howto_step_7_des: Submit a test answer from a phone on mobile data, then open the database and read the row it created. Look for anything that identifies the sender, like an IP address or an exact time, and remove it. Then read the reply as the writer would.

plan.angle: The live results are Typeform, Jotform and LimeSurvey templates, a SurveyHero sign-up page, a SurveyMonkey question list, a Laserfiche routing form and a Reddit thread from an academic hunting for a tool. They hand over questions and a share link. People Also Ask is almost all one worry: can an anonymous survey be traced, and does Google Forms or SurveyMonkey really hide who answered. This page answers that worry with mechanics: what the form must never store (name, email, sign-in, IP address, exact time), how small groups stay hidden, and how someone gets a reply without being identified, shown in four settings searchers have: a restaurant staff suggestion box, upward feedback on managers, mid-semester course feedback and an HOA board.
tab_stories: Saltbrook Kitchen's 3 restaurants share one staff suggestion form with no name or email field, no sign-in and no IP address saved, and each submitter gets a case code such as PINE-4417 to read the general manager's reply.

Tallgrass Analytics collects feedback on its 9 managers each spring and fall, a report stays hidden until at least 4 direct reports have answered, and Theo Lund's team of 5 has 3 answers so his report is held.

Dr. Lena Ortiz runs anonymous midterm feedback for Statistics 210, the form keeps the date of each answer but not the time, and when it closes on Friday 31 of 42 students have answered with problem set length raised in 14 comments.

Larkspur Commons, an HOA of 120 homes, checks each resident comment against the resident directory before the monthly board digest, and a comment that names a neighbor is held for the community manager to edit.
